idiom_name: one table + type-code column + per-class mapper/factory
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create one table whose columns are the union of the hierarchy's fields plus a discriminator column holding a value per concrete class (integer or short text - never a class name unless the language's ORM already uses one). Give each class a mapper that reads/writes only its own columns, always writes its discriminator value on insert, and filters reads by it; a factory switches on the discriminator to instantiate the right class behind the base type. Make the discriminator explicit data (name, type and value per class) rather than a framework default, add a CHECK constraint where the database can connect the type code to the columns it requires, and index the discriminator if single-subtype queries are common. Keep subtype fields nullable and treat 'unknown discriminator' as an error, not an empty object.
code_sketch:
CREATE TABLE employee (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  type    TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('employee','engineer','manager')),
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  language TEXT,      -- engineer only
  reports  INTEGER,   -- manager only
  CHECK (type <> 'engineer' OR language IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (type <> 'manager'  OR reports  IS NOT NULL)
);
-- mapper: SELECT * FROM employee WHERE type = ? AND id = ?
-- factory: switch (row.type) { ... default: throw unknown_discriminator }
pitfalls: Skipping the discriminator discipline (raw UPDATEs, imports, other services) leaves rows whose type code contradicts their populated columns; the mapper then instantiates the wrong class or fails at read time.
Letting the table grow into a union of weakly related subtypes - the classic sign that class-table inheritance was the right choice.
No bound on column count and no per-subtype index plan: subtype queries degrade while the shared table keeps widening.

Wrong move: relying on nullable columns alone to express subtype fields -> the schema can no longer enforce 'every engineer row has a language', and rows violating subtype invariants flow into the application and fail deep in domain code -> instead add CHECK constraints tying the discriminator to the columns its type requires (or move to class-table inheritance once those constraints are real requirements).

Wrong move: accepting the framework's default discriminator values (Rails writes the Ruby class name into type; EF Core stores the .NET type name) -> renaming or namespacing a class silently changes what is written to disk and old rows become unloadable or materialise as the wrong type -> instead pin explicit discriminator values in the mapping metadata and treat them as a stable, reviewed contract.

Wrong move: running bulk data migrations through the polymorphic model classes -> Rails-style ORMs load unintended subclass logic and implicit type filters during migrations, rewriting or skipping the wrong rows -> instead migrate with plain SQL or a non-inheriting schema-only model bound to the raw table, as GitLab's database guide mandates for STI tables.
